verses.text: Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, after the abominations of the nations whom Yahweh cast out before the children of Israel.
For he built again the high places which Hezekiah his father had broken down; and he raised up altars for the Baals, made Asheroth, and worshiped all the army of the sky, and served them.
He built altars in Yahweh’s house, of which Yahweh said, “My name shall be in Jerusalem forever.”
He built altars for all the army of the sky in the two courts of Yahweh’s house.

He also made his children to pass through the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom. He practiced sorcery, divination, and witchcraft, and dealt with those who had familiar spirits, and with wizards. He did much evil in Yahweh’s sight, to provoke him to anger.

He set the engraved image of the idol, which he had made, in God’s house, of which God said to David and to Solomon his son, “In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, will I put my name forever.

I will not any more remove the foot of Israel from off the land which I have appointed for your fathers, if only they will observe to do all that I have commanded them, even all the law, the statutes, and the ordinances given by Moses.”
Manasseh seduced Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that they did more evil than the nations whom Yahweh destroyed before the children of Israel did.
Yahweh spoke to Manasseh, and to his people; but they didn’t listen.
Therefore Yahweh brought on them the captains of the army of the king of Assyria, who took Manasseh in chains, bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon.
When he was in distress, he begged Yahweh his God, and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers.
He prayed to him; and he was entreated by him, and heard his supplication, and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that Yahweh was God.

Now after this, he built an outer wall to David’s city, on the west side of Gihon, in the valley, even to the entrance at the fish gate. He encircled Ophel with it, and raised it up to a very great height; and he put valiant captains in all the fortified cities of Judah.
He took away the foreign gods, and the idol out of Yahweh’s house, and all the altars that he had built in the mountain of Yahweh’s house, and in Jerusalem, and cast them out of the city.
He built up Yahweh’s altar, and offered sacrifices of peace offerings and of thanksgiving on it, and commanded Judah to serve Yahweh, the God of Israel.
Nevertheless the people sacrificed still in the high places, but only to Yahweh their God.

Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and his prayer to his God, and the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of Yahweh, the God of Israel, behold, they are written among the acts of the kings of Israel.

His prayer also, and how God was entreated of him, and all his sin and his trespass, and the places in which he built high places, and set up the Asherah poles and the engraved images, before he humbled himself: behold, they are written in the history of Hozai.
So Manasseh slept with his fathers, and they buried him in his own house; and Amon his son reigned in his place.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign; and he reigned two years in Jerusalem.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, as did Manasseh his father; and Amon sacrificed to all the engraved images which Manasseh his father had made, and served them.
He didn’t humble himself before Yahweh, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself; but this same Amon trespassed more and more.
His servants conspired against him, and put him to death in his own house.
But the people of the land killed all those who had conspired against king Amon; and the people of the land made Josiah his son king in his place.

footnotes.content: Manasseh took the throne as a boy—twelve years old with the weight of a kingdom on his small shoulders. That's when hearts are most easily led astray, when no one has yet taught them the fear of the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's a boy who chooses the very evil his grandfather Hezekiah had torn down. I've seen that pattern—a generation inherits freedom but forgets why it cost so much. Manasseh had the history in front of him and chose to turn away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He doesn't just tolerate the high places; he rebuilds them. And he doesn't stop there—he bows to Baal, serves the sky itself. There's a hunger in that kind of rebellion, isn't there? As if idolatry could satisfy what only the Lord can fill.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Manasseh defiles the very house where the Lord promised His name would dwell forever. The audacity is almost unbearable—to take the place of covenant and make it a monument to your own darkness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He fills even the courtyards—public spaces—with altars to false gods. His idolatry isn't hidden shame; it's a proclamation. That's how far a young king can wander when pride hardens his heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The horror deepens: he passes his own children through fire, turns to sorcery and witchcraft. When a heart turns fully from God, watch how quickly evil multiplies. The father's rebellion becomes the family's curse.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He places an idol—a carved thing—right in God's house, the very house God promised would hold His name forever. It's the final insult: turning the promise of God into a mockery.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is God's ancient word to David and Solomon: 'I have appointed this land for you—if you keep my law.' Manasseh heard this promise, I'm sure of it. Yet he stepped over it like it meant nothing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A king's heart shapes his people's heart. Manasseh led Judah deeper into evil than even the pagan nations around them—and God had driven those nations out for their wickedness. The student had become worse than his teachers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord spoke. Again and again, I imagine—through prophets, through conscience, through the witness of His people. But Manasseh wouldn't listen. Sometimes the Lord's mercy is simply that He keeps speaking to us, even when we refuse to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Assyrians come with chains. In Manasseh's pride, he likely never imagined he could fall so far—from king on his throne to captive bound in fetters, carried away to Babylon. Yet sometimes exile is mercy wearing a harsh face.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: And here—here is where the broken king turns. In distress, stripped of all power and pretense, he begs the God he had scorned. Humility in chains: sometimes the Lord lets us lose everything so we might find Him again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo of grace: a man who turned to dust finds himself lifted and restored. Manasseh's prayer is heard. God brings him home. In this, every broken heart glimpses what the Father does—He bends to listen when we finally cry out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He returns and builds—not for himself, but for the city's defense. He strengthens what had been neglected, posts captains in the fortified cities. Repentance is never just feeling sorry; it's turning around and building something better.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He tears down what he had built, casts out the idols he once treasured. Every false god he had raised up now leaves his hands. Repentance is costly—it means undoing the very things our pride invested in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He rebuilds the Lord's altar and offers sacrifices of thanksgiving. Notice: thanksgiving, not just atonement. He's not paying a debt; he's a man amazed at grace. He calls Judah to serve the God who had never abandoned him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people still sacrifice on the high places—old habits die hard. Yet now they do so only to the Lord, not to idols. It's an imperfect reform, incomplete. Manasseh has turned his kingdom, but the heart-work takes generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His prayer and his restoration are recorded among the acts of the kings of Israel. A man's repentance can be written into history—a record that the Lord hears, that mercy is real, that turning around is possible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even his humbling is preserved—how he was entreated, how he confessed his sin and his idolatry before the correction came. The chronicler is saying: Yes, his evil was great; and yes, his repentance was true. Both are written.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Manasseh dies and is buried in his own house—not in the royal tombs, but still at home, still among his own. He reigned fifty-five years, much of it lost to evil, yet the last years marked by restoration. A long life that teaches us it's never too late to turn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amon begins to reign—a young man of twenty-two, inheriting his father's throne after Manasseh's repentance. Will the son learn from the father's fall? The text will answer that question quickly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amon does evil, and his evil is a step backward—he serves the very idols his father had torn down. The child didn't learn from the father's captivity; he inherited only the rebellion, not the repentance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Unlike Manasseh, Amon refuses to humble himself. He sees his father's fall and doesn't bend the knee; he trespasses more and more. How tragic—to watch grace work in one generation and refuse it in the next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His own servants conspire and kill him in his own house. A king who spurns God becomes powerless to protect himself, even within his own walls. Pride goes before destruction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people of the land undo the conspiracy and make Josiah king—Amon's young son. They turn away from Amon's path, searching for a different kind of leadership. Here is hope again: the people still remember, and they choose a new direction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
